content: 1. General Disorders and Administration Site Conditions: Fluid retention and a general feeling of malaise have been reported. 2. Hepatobiliary Disorders: Cases of cholecystitis (inflammation of the gallbladder) have been observed. 3. Investigations: Increased blood pressure and lipid disorders have been noted. 4. Musculoskeletal and Connective Tissue Disorders: Muscle spasms have been reported. 5. Psychiatric Disorders: Insomnia, decreased libido, and increased libido have been documented. 6. Reproductive System and Breast Disorders: Galactorrhea (milk production not associated with breastfeeding), genital discharge, premenstrual syndrome, uterine spasms, vaginal discharge, and vulvovaginal dryness have been observed. 7. Respiratory, Thoracic, and Mediastinal Disorders: Pulmonary embolism has been reported. 8. Skin and Subcutaneous Tissue Disorders: Chloasma (skin discoloration), contact dermatitis, erythema, and skin irritation have been noted. Postmarketing Experience Adverse reactions identified during post-approval use of norelgestromin and ethinyl estradiol include those reported voluntarily. Due to the voluntary nature of these reports and the uncertain population size, it is not always possible to reliably estimate their frequency or establish a causal relationship to drug exposure. Drug Interactions Interactions with Concurrently Used Drugs: Refer to the labeling of other drugs used alongside hormonal contraceptives to understand potential interactions or enzyme alterations. Substances Decreasing Plasma Concentrations of Combined Hormonal Contraceptives (CHCs): Drugs or herbal products that induce enzymes, such as cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4), may reduce CHC plasma concentrations, potentially diminishing their effectiveness or increasing breakthrough bleeding. Examples include phenytoin, barbiturates, carbamazepine, bosentan, felbamate, griseofulvin, oxcarbazepine, rifampicin, topiramate, rifabutin, rufinamide, aprepitant, and St. John’s wort. Women should be counseled to use alternative or backup contraception when enzyme inducers are used with CHCs and to continue backup contraception for 28 days after discontinuing the enzyme inducer. Substances Increasing Plasma Concentrations of CHCs: Co-administration of atorvastatin or rosuvastatin with certain CHCs containing ethinyl estradiol (EE) can increase EE plasma levels by approximately 20–25%. Ascorbic acid and acetaminophen may increase EE plasma concentrations, possibly by inhibiting conjugation. CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as itraconazole, voriconazole, fluconazole, grapefruit juice, or ketoconazole, may elevate plasma hormone concentrations. HIV/HCV Protease Inhibitors and Non-Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors: Significant changes in plasma concentrations of estrogen and/or progestin (increase or decrease) have been observed with co-administration of HIV protease inhibitors, HCV protease inhibitors, or non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors. Other Drug Interactions: CHCs may increase plasma concentrations of drugs like cyclosporine, prednisolone, theophylline, tizanidine, and voriconazole. CHCs may decrease plasma concentrations of acetaminophen, clofibric acid, morphine, salicylic acid, and temazepam. Significant reductions in lamotrigine plasma concentrations have been observed, likely due to induction of lamotrigine glucuronidation, which may reduce seizure control. Dosage adjustments of lamotrigine may be necessary. Thyroid Hormone Replacement Therapy: Women on thyroid hormone replacement therapy may require increased doses of thyroid hormone due to increased serum concentrations of thyroid-binding globulin with CHC use. Interference with Laboratory Tests The use of contraceptive steroids may influence the results of certain laboratory tests, including coagulation factors, lipids, glucose tolerance, and binding proteins. Use in Specific Populations Pregnancy: There is little or no increased risk of birth defects in women who inadvertently use hormonal contraceptives during early pregnancy. Epidemiologic studies and meta-analyses have not found an increased risk of genital or non-genital birth defects (including cardiac anomalies and limb reduction defects) following exposure to low-dose hormonal contraceptives before conception or during early pregnancy. Hormonal contraceptives should not be used during pregnancy to treat threatened or habitual abortion. Labor and Delivery: There is no FDA guidance on the use of norelgestromin and ethinyl estradiol transdermal systems during labor and delivery. Nursing Mothers: The effects of ORTHO EVRA in nursing mothers have not been evaluated. Estrogen-containing CHCs can reduce milk production in breastfeeding mothers, though this is less likely once breastfeeding is well-established. However, it can occur at any time in some women. Small amounts of contraceptive steroids and/or metabolites are present in breast milk. Pediatric Use: Safety and efficacy of ORTHO EVRA have been established in women of reproductive age. Efficacy is expected to be the same for post-pubertal adolescents under 18 and users 18 years and older. Use of this product before menarche is not indicated. Geriatric Use: ORTHO EVRA has not been studied in postmenopausal women and is not indicated for this population. Gender: There is no FDA guidance on the use of norelgestromin and ethinyl estradiol transdermal systems with respect to specific gender populations. Race: There is no FDA guidance on the use of norelgestromin and ethinyl estradiol transdermal systems with respect to specific racial populations. Renal Impairment: No studies with ORTHO EVRA have been conducted in women with renal impairment. Hepatic Impairment: No studies with ORTHO EVRA have been conducted in women with hepatic impairment. Steroid hormones may be poorly metabolized in patients with impaired liver function. Acute or chronic disturbances of liver function may necessitate discontinuation of CHC use until liver function markers return to normal and CHC causation is excluded.
